etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English stove.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English sweater.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese of unclear derivation:
* Probably originally a compound of 吾 (a, Eastern Old Japanese first-person pronoun) + の (no, possessive particle) + 兄 (ye → e, “eldest sibling”, see below):
*: ⟨a no₂ ye⟩ → */anʉʲɨe/ → /ani/
* Alternatively, an apophonic form of 姉 (ane, “elder sister”), itself possibly from the same derivation above.
* Several other theories have also been suggested.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*/kwæi/ → /kʷæi/ → /keː/
From Middle Chinese 兄 (MC xjwaeng).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/je/ → /e/
From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese.
Originally a compound of 子 (ko, “child”) + の (no, possessive particle) + 上 (kami, “upper”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨puyu⟩ → /ɸuju/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *puyu.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 冬 (MC towng).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb せく (seku, “to cough”). Cognate with 堰 (seki, “dam”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 処(か) (ka, “place”) + 重(へ) (he, “division”), in reference to walls dividing objects apart. The he changes to be as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨imo₁⟩ → */imʷo/ → /imo/
From Old Japanese 妹 (imo₁). First cited in the Kojiki of 712.
Speculatively, may be related to terms such as 女 (me₁, womi₁na, “woman”), 嫗 (omi₁na, “elderly woman”), and 母 (omo, “mother”), wherein the medial /-m-/ appears to signify woman, female. However, the difference in vowel values presents a difficulty.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/imo ɸito/ → /imowito/ → */imowuto/ → /imoːto/
Originally a compound of 妹 (imo, “sister, close female companion”) + 人 (hito, “person”). First cited in The Tales of Ise of the early 900s.
This is an instance of ウ音便 (u onbin, “u sound shift”), found in terms with bilabial consonants (/m/, /b/, /w/) followed by i; commonly seen in terms such as 玄人 (kurōto, “professional”), 素人 (shirōto, “amateur”), or possibly, 相撲 (sumō, “sumo”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Analyzed as a shortening of imōto, itself a compound 妹 (imo, “sister, close female companion”) + 人 (hito, “person”).
Appears in The Tale of Heiji, written around the mid-12th century. May be much older, as this reading is also included in kun'yomi glosses for the Nihon Shoki of 720 (although the manuscripts with the glosses themselves are not as old).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 妹 (MC mwojH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese of unclear derivation:
* Probably originally a compound of 吾 (a, Eastern Old Japanese first-person pronoun) + の (no, possessive particle) + 兄 (ye → e, “eldest sibling”):
*: ⟨a no₂ ye⟩ → */anʉʲɨe/ → /ane/
* An apophonic form of 兄 (ani, “elder brother”).
* Several other theories have also been suggested.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ipe₁⟩ → /ipʲe/ → /iɸe/ → /iwe/ → /ie/
From Old Japanese. Possibly cognate with Old Korean 邑勒 (iprʌk, “house”).
Possibly related to 廬 (iho → io, “temporary hut”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Inherited from Old Japanese [Term?], from Proto-Japonic *utui.
Doublet of 内(うち) (uchi, “middle, inside”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Contraction of uchi above.
Often following the genitive case marker の (no) which contracts to -n.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 家 (MC kae).
The 漢音 (kan'on, literally “Han sound”), so likely a latter borrowing from Middle Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 家 (MC kae).
The 呉音 (goon, literally “Wu sound”), so likely the initial borrowing from Middle Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Early Middle Japanese adjective 寒(さむ)し (samushi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in き (ki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of い (i).
Starting in at least the Muromachi period, this term became sporadically pronounced with a medial /b/ as 寒(さぶ)し (sabushi) (not to be confused with 寂(さぶ)し (sabushi), original form of 寂(さび)しい (sabishii)). Compare the similar /m/~/b/ alternation seen in 寂しい (sabishii, samishii, “lonely, desolate”), 頭 (tsuburi, tsumuri, “head”), and 煙 (keburi, kemuri, “smoke”). Related to 冷(さ)む (samu, “to cool down”), modern 冷(さ)める (sameru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Attested in the 日(に)本(ほん)書(しょ)紀(き) (Nihon Shoki), completed in 720 and one of the earliest works written in Japanese, with a meaning of “bed”.
According to the 和(わ)句(く)解(げ) (Wakuge), published in 1668 by early Edo-period scholar 松(まつ)永(なが)貞(てい)徳(とく) (Matsunaga Teitoku), derives from 行(ゆ)か (yuka), the 未(み)然(ぜん)形(けい) (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) stem of the verb 行(ゆ)く (yuku, “to go”), of an original meaning similar to “not going”, in reference to a place where one sits down to rest.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨to₂ko₂⟩ → /toko/
From Old Japanese. Cognate with 所 (tokoro, “place”). Attested since at least the Nara period, appearing in the Man'yōshū, completed in 759.
Possibly an ancient compound of ⟨to₁⟩ (Proto-Japonic *to (“place”), as in 跡 ⟨ato₁⟩, “footprint, track”, from “foot place, where one has stepped”) + ⟨ko₂⟩ (noun-forming suffixing element denoting “place”, as in ここ ⟨ko₂ko₂⟩, “here”, from “this place”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ʑau/ → /ɕau/ → /ɕɔː/ → /ɕoː/
From Middle Chinese 床 (MC dzrjang). Devoicing apparently occurred after borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Short for earlier 見(み)せ棚(だな) (misedana), from 見(み)せる (miseru, “to show”) + 棚(たな) (tana, “shelf”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 店 (MC temH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/posi/ → /ɸoɕi/ → /hoɕi/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pəsi.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 星 (MC seng).
The Singapore sense derives from the pre-World War Two kanji spelling 星加坡 (modern kanji spelling 新加坡) as borrowed from Chinese, itself a transliteration of Malay Singapura.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 昨夜 (MC dzak yaeH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Shift from 夕べ (yūbe, “evening”), which has an additional 平板型 (heiban-gata) or [0] accent pitch.
The kanji spelling is from sakuya above.
Cognate with Northern Amami Ōshima ゆぶぃ (yubï, “last night”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/juɸube/ → */juːbe/ → /junbe/ → /jumbe/
Shift from yūbe above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The kanji spelling is from sakuya above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/jobe/ → */joːbe/ → /jonbe/ → /jombe/
Shift from yobe above.
The kanji spelling is from sakuya above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨tuki₂⟩ → */tukɨ/ → */t͡sukɨ/ → /t͡suki/
From Old Japanese 月 (tuki₂), ultimately from Proto-Japonic *tukui.
For the vowel alternation, see WT:AJPX#Standalone forms and combining forms.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ɡʷatɨ/ → /ɡʷat͡su/ → /ɡat͡su/
From Middle Chinese 月 (ŋʉɐt̚).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ɡʷetu/ → /ɡet͡su/
From Middle Chinese 月 (ŋʉɐt̚).
Compare modern Hakka 月 (ngie̍t), Min Nan 月 (ge̍h).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ɡʷat͡ɕi/ → /ɡat͡ɕi/
First attested in the Edo period.
Appears to be a poetic use of the 呉(ご)音(おん) (goon, literally “Wu sound”) reading, in reference to a rank of 端(はし)女(じょ)郎(ろう) (hashi jorō, “low-end prostitute]”) in the Kansai region. According to a popular song, a 月(がち) (gachi, “moon”) prostitute cost one 匁(もんめ) (monme, old unit of currency, worth roughly 3.75 grams of silver), a 影(かげ) (kage, “shadow”) prostitute cost two monme, and a 汐(しお) (shio, “tide; loveliness”) prostitute cost three monme.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Either a shift in sense from the low-ranking prostitute meaning above, or a shift in pronunciation from 頑(がん)痴(ち) (ganchi, literally “stubborn and stupid”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 正月 (MC tsyeng ngjwot)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese papa, in turn traced to Proto-Japonic *papa.
/haha/: */papa/ → /fafa/ → /fawa/ → /fafa/ → /haha/.
First cited to a portion of the Shoku Nihongi dated to 729, with the phonetic spelling 婆婆 (papa).
Medial /f/ [ɸ] regularly changes to /w/ [ɰᵝ], resulting in /fawa/ → /hawa/, the expected final form; see hawa below. This form first appears in the Heian period. However, likely due to spelling influence or reduplication associations, the earlier /fafa/ resurfaced in the late 16th century towards the end of the Muromachi period, with both forms seen until recent times, when hawa falls into disuse. Initial /f-/ [ɸ] regularly becomes [h], resulting in modern [ha̠ha̠].

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, the phonologically expected development. See etymology for haha above for details.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Possibly an abbreviation of haha, or possibly the original form.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Obsolete and unused in modern Japanese. Already falling into disuse by the writing of the Man'yōshū in 759, where it is only found in pieces written in eastern dialects. Possibly cognate with Korean 엄마 (eomma, “mother”), 어머니 (eomeoni, “mother”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Obsolete and unused in modern Japanese. Appears to be an alteration from amo above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Unknown. One theory holds that this is a corrupted and abbreviated form of 御方様 (okatasama), a term to refer to or address someone else's wife (now extremely formal, but much more everyday in the Edo period), possibly influenced by children's speech.
/okatasama/ → /katasama/ → /kakasama/ → /kaka/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Alteration of kaka: /kaka/ → /-kka/ → /kaː/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ko₂pori⟩ → */kəpori/ → /koɸori/ → /kowori/ → /koːri/
From Old Japanese.
The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 凍(こお)る (kōru, “to freeze”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨pi₁⟩ → */pʲi/ → /ɸi/ → /hi/
From Old Japanese. Attested in the Man'yōshū of circa 759 CE.
Possibly cognate with 冷える (hieru, “to become cold”).
Compare Middle Chinese 冰 (MC ping).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 冰 (MC ping).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *yu.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. Also used in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Baby talk. Possibly onomatopoeic of a person blowing on a hot beverage.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨pi₂⟩ → */pʷɨ/ → /ɸi/ → /hi/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *poy.
Apophonic form of ho (see below). Compare 木 (ki, ko-, “tree”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/po/ → /ɸo/ → /ho/
From Old Japanese.
Combining form of hi above. Probably the oldest form, possibly cognate with Korean 불 (bul, “fire”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kwa/ → /ka/
From Middle Chinese 火 (MC xwaX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨po no₂ po⟩ → */ponəpo/ → /ɸonoɸo/ → /ɸonowo/ → /honowo/ → /hono.o/
From Old Japanese 炎 (pono₂po).
Compound of 火 (ho, combining form of hi, “fire”) + の (no, possessive particle) + 穂 (ho, “ear (of grain)”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 火 (ho, “fire”, combining form) + 群 (mura, “gathering, group”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/emʉ/ → /eɴ/
From Middle Chinese 炎 (MC hjem).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 炎 is a daiyōji replacing 焔.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/keburi/ → /kemuri/
Shift from Old Japanese-derived keburi reading (see below) as a regular /b/ → /m/ change. Appears in the Taiheiki of the late 1300s.
Now the most common reading.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kemuri/ → /kemu/
Clipping of earlier kemuri.
Attested since at least 1275.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 煙る (keburu, “to be smoky, to give off smoke”). Appears with this reading in the Man'yōshū.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Clipping of earlier keburi.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 煙 (MC 'en).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 父 (titi), from Proto-Japonic *titi.
Still in modern usage.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Appears in the Utsubo Monogatari of roughly 970 CE.
Glossed as “I[gualmente], chichi. Pay” (“same as chichi. Father”) in Nippo Jisho.
Shift from chichi.
Usage continued until at least the early 1700s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Appears in the Nippo Jisho of 1603.
Originally a shift from chichi or tete in baby talk, used by children to refer to their own father.
Still in modern usage.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/totosan/ → /totːɕan/ → /t͡ɕan/
Likely a contraction of 父さん (toto-san).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The “father” and “uncle” affixes is from Middle Chinese 父 (MC bjuX).
The “old man” affix is from Middle Chinese 父 (MC pjuX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From a corruption of Middle Chinese 父 (MC pjuX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨kaso₂⟩ → */kasə/ → /kaso/ → /kazo/
From Old Japanese. Appears in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE as unvoiced kaso. Further derivation unknown.
May have fallen out of use by 1603, when neither kaso nor kazo are found in the Nippo Jisho. Kaso would be here as the sixth entry from the bottom on the left, and kazo would be here as the eighth from the bottom on the right.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *‹u,o›si.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 牛 (ngjuw, “cow”). Compare Hokkien 牛 (giû / ngiû).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *enu. Derivation uncertain. Various theories exist, including derivation from ancient verb 往ぬ (inu, “to leave, to be gone”), from the way a dog will guard the house while the master is away; from a compound of 家 (ie, “house, home”) + 寝 (nu, “to sleep”, ancient monosyllabic form of modern 寝る neru); from ancient Japanese 狗 (enu < wenu, “puppy, dog”), itself of uncertain derivation; or as a borrowing from some other unknown language.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨neko₁⟩ → /neko/
From Old Japanese. Cognate with Miyako にか (nika, “cat”, Tarama and Minna dialects) via unknown Japonic substratum.
Listed in modern references as a compound of ね (ne, onomatopoeia of the sound a cat makes; compare modern Japanese にゃ (nya), English mew, meow) + こ (ko, diminutive noun-forming suffix). According to the 和(わ)名(みょう)類(るい)聚(じゅ)抄(しょう) (Wamyō Ruijushō) of 931–938, neko is a shortening of 猫(ねこま) (nekoma), but neko appears in texts earlier than nekoma: neko is first attested in the Shin'yaku Kegonkyō Ongi Shiki of 794, while nekoma is not attested until 918 in the 本(ほん)草(ぞう)和(わ)名(みょう) (Honzō Wamyō, the oldest surviving dictionary of medicine in Japan).
A comparison of accent patterns between the dialects shows some confusion (see dialectal data):
* One group of dialects behaves as if was the Heian Kyoto accent pattern: many dialects with the Tokyo type accent, including the standard Japanese in Tokyo, pronounce this word with an pitch pattern, and in some non-mainstream Keihan type dialects as well, this word has a corresponding pitch pattern.
* Another group of dialects behaves as if was the Heian Kyoto accent pattern: the mainstream Keihan type dialects pronounce this word with an pitch pattern, and in a few of the Tokyo type dialects, this word has a corresponding pitch pattern.
As a result, this term is one example of words that have the same pitch accent pattern between Tokyo and Osaka/Kyoto. The confusion seems to be due to an impression that the term comes from a compound word origin.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
According to the 和(わ)名(みょう)類(るい)聚(じゅ)抄(しょう) (Wamyō Ruijushō) of 931–938, the term 猫(ねこ) (neko) is a shortening of nekoma.
:
:
猫: 野王案、猫、音苗、禰古麻、下總本有和名二字興河海抄引此合、本草和名同訓、或省云禰古、新撰字鏡、狸、禰古、按狸一名猫、見本草和名、似虎而小、熊捕鼠為糧
Cat. According to Yewang, cat, sound-reading myō, [Japanese reading] nekoma; later compendia have a two character Japanese name - perhaps the Rivers and Seas Annotations references this compilation, the Honzō wamyō [has] a kun homophone, certain omissions call it 'neko', [in the] Shinsen Jikyō 'tanuki' - [read] neko, to check 'tanuki' [as] one name [for] a cat - see the Honzō wamyō; like a tiger but small, the creature catches rats for food
However, nekoma is first cited to 918 in the 本(ほん)草(ぞう)和(わ)名(みょう) (Honzō Wamyō, the oldest surviving dictionary of medicine in Japan), while 猫(ねこ) (neko) is first attested earlier in the Shin'yaku Kegonkyō Ongi Shiki of 794.
:
:
家狸、一名猫、和名禰古末
A house raccoon; also called a cat; the Japanese name is nekoma.
One theory about the derivation describes the first mora ⟨ne⟩ as onomatopoeia for the sound a cat makes, compare modern Japanese にゃ (nya), English mew, meow. The last two morae ⟨ko₁ma⟩ might accord with 熊(くま) (kuma, “bear”) if it were from Proto-Japonic *koma (class 2.3 ), in the sense of "four-legged animal". However, Japanese kuma appears to have cognates in ancient Koreanic sources meaning specifically "bear" (see the 熊(くま) (kuma, “bear”) entry for further details), making this theory less likely.
The Heian Kyoto accent of this word is ; note that in compound words for species names, the pitch pattern may be simplified to <-HL> when the final element is a 2-mora noun (e.g. 青(あお)海(の)苔(り) (aonori ← àwònórì ← *àwò-nòrì, “green laver”), and the presence or absence of this phenomenon could explain the accent confusion in neko.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kankami.
Originally a compound of 影 (kaga, ancient combining form of 影 (kage), “shadow; outline; figure; image”) + 見 (mi, “seeing”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of verb 見る (miru), “to see, to look at”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/kjau/ → /kjɔː/ → /kjoː/
From Middle Chinese 鏡 (MC kjaengH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨yuki₁⟩ → */jukʲi/ → /juki/
From Old Japanese. Found in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.
Also found once in the Man'yōshū in a so-called 東歌 (Azuma uta, literally “eastern song”) in the eastern dialect of Old Japanese, realized as ⟨yo₂ki₁⟩.
Reconstructed by some as deriving from Proto-Japonic *yoki.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨kutu⟩: */kutu/ → /kut͡su/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kutu. Cognate with Yaeyama 草鞋 (futsï), Yonaguni 草鞋 (c'i).
Found in the Man'yōshū poetry compilation, completed circa 759.
Ultimate derivation unclear. Some Japanese sources suggest a borrowing from or cognate with Korean 구두 (gudu, “shoes”), but then some Korean sources suggest that the Korean term was borrowed from Japanese 靴 (kutsu, “shoes”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
The initial m sound was apparently emphasized, possibly similar to *mma, becoming then uma or muma, via processes also seen in the word 梅 (ume, mume, “plum”). However, Pellard simply reconstructs Proto-Japonic *uma and treats the mentioned processes as secondary.
The ma sound denoting "horse" is common to a number of languages of central Asia, where horses were first domesticated, which has led some to speculate about a possible cognate root (but no consensus on any kind of relation exists). Compare Manchu ᠮᠣᡵᡳᠨ (morin, “horse”), Mongolian морь (morʹ, “horse”), Korean 말 (mal, “horse”), Mandarin 馬 /马 (mǎ, “horse”), and Proto-Indo-European *márkos (“horse”) and descendants such as Irish marc (“horse”, archaic) or English mare (“female horse”). More at *márkos.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from uma form, becoming more common starting from the Heian Period. This change later reverted, and muma is now considered obsolete.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Possibly from preform *Nma; ultimately from Proto-Japonic *Cma.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Possibly from preform *MCma; ultimately from Proto-Japonic *Cma.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 馬 (MC maeX). The 漢音 (kan'on), so a later borrowing. Compare Min Nan 馬 /马 (bé, bée, má) where some of the readings show a shift from initial nasal /m-/ to voiced plosive /b-/.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨to₂ri⟩ → /tori/
From Old Japanese. Attested in the Kojiki of 712 with the phonetic spelling 登理 (⟨to₂ri⟩, /təri/). In turn, reconstructed as inherited from Proto-Japonic *təri. Possibly cognate with Middle Korean ᄃᆞᆰ (tolk), modern Korean 닭 (dak, “fowl; chicken”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨to₂ri⟩ → ⟨*to₂⟩ → /to/
From Old Japanese. Appears to be a shift from tori above.
